bio.en: Tamar Yehoshua is president of product and technology at Glean, previously CPO at Slack (where she 10x'd revenue through IPO and Salesforce acquisition) and a long-time Google leader on Search.
bio.zh: Tamar Yehoshua 是 Glean 的产品与技术总裁，此前曾任 Slack 首席产品官（在她任内营收增长 10 倍，直至 IPO 并被 Salesforce 收购），也是 Google 搜索领域的长期领导者。

summary.en: Tamar discusses what it takes to lead product and technology at a fast-scaling enterprise AI company like Glean, and the lessons from scaling Slack 10x and leading Search at Google. She covers how to build trustworthy AI products for enterprises, the interplay of product and engineering leadership, and how to maintain quality and momentum through hypergrowth. The episode is a senior operator's view of building serious enterprise software.
summary.zh: Tamar 探讨了在像 Glean 这样快速扩张的企业级 AI 公司中，领导产品与技术需要什么，以及从 Slack 十倍增长、在 Google 领导搜索中学到的经验。她涵盖了如何为企业打造值得信赖的 AI 产品、产品与工程领导力的相互作用，以及如何在超高速增长中保持品质与势头。本期是一位资深运营者对打造严肃企业级软件的透视。

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: Make sure you go somewhere where you have a good engineering partner. Because if you have great ideas of what to build but you can't get them built, then you go nowhere. So that has to be part of your evaluation criteria that you meet and value your engineering partner before you join. And then I think what's really important is that you're aligned. You understand your roles and responsibilities and where you're going to divide and conquer and where you're going to be aligned. You don't want any of this ... Like people in the organization, they ask mom, they asked dad and they got different opinions and playing one against the other. That doesn't work.
turns.zh: 一定要确保你选择的合作伙伴在工程领域表现出色。因为如果你有绝佳的创意，却无法将其变为现实，那你注定一事无成。因此，在加入新公司之前，你必须评估并重视与工程团队的合作关系。另外，我认为最重要的是要保持团队的协同一致。你们要明确各自的角色与职责，清楚如何合理分工与协作，确保目标一致。切忌出现团队成员各自为政、意见不一、相互扯皮的情况——这种局面注定失败。

turns.speaker: Lenny

She also spent five years at Amazon as director of engineering and vice president at A9.com. She was also a venture partner at IVP and has been on board of directors for ServiceNow, Snyk, RetailMeNot, and Yext. turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: One of the things that I think is overlooked is do a really good job at whatever your job is at that point. People have a tendency ... Especially product managers are very ambitious and they want to get to the next level and they're always eyeing the next job, but you're not going to get the next job unless you do really well at the job that you're in. Knock it out of the park. However simple, however easy it may be to you, do a great job. And in tech jobs, there's table stakes. There's table stakes of you need to be technical, you need to know the latest technology, you need to understand your product, the product you're working on. No matter what your role is. You have to understand it deeply. You need to understand metrics. So especially product managers have a wide breadth of things that they need to understand. So those are a given. You need to do that.
turns.zh: 我认为被忽视的一件事是，尽可能出色地完成手头的工作。人们往往……尤其是产品经理们雄心勃勃，渴望晋升到更高职位，总是在关注下一个工作机会。但除非你能把当前的工作做得极其出色，否则你根本无法获得下一个机会。要做到卓越。无论工作多么简单、多么容易，都要出色完成。在科技行业，基本要求就是你必须具备技术能力、掌握最新技术、深入理解产品。无论你的角色是什么，都必须做到这些。同时，还要精通指标分析。因此，产品经理需要掌握的知识面极为广泛。这是基本要求，你必须达标。

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: So now the question is the difference in leadership and executive roles and when you're getting there. So how do you start transitioning? So after you've done a great job at everything and you understand the core skills that you need, another thing you really need to know is understanding people and motivations. And when you're building products, you have to understand why does somebody want to use your product? What problem are they solving? Why do they want to click on that button? What's going to make them feel good when they click on it? What's going to give them delight and what's also going to make them feel bad and frustrated and what do they not want to do? So you need to understand motivations in people for building products and for building teams and organizations. So just like why does somebody want to click on a button, why does somebody want to join your team? Why do they want to work hard? What are they trying to accomplish? What's the goal for their career? (00:06:54): So you have to be able to read people, ask lots of questions to understand them. And I'll say one thing that really helped me, this is a strange segue, but my father was a psychiatrist and when I was growing up, we would have family occasions, go to events, whatever, and afterwards in the car ride back, he would always give his perspective of analyzing what happened at the event. What this person was thinking. Why did they say this? And then he would quiz me of, "Why do you think they did that?" And it was really interesting because it taught me to see the whole room. To see how people react. Like Lenny, if you say something and somebody else is there, look at the other person. What's their face saying? You can understand so much if you're paying attention. So I think when you want to build for people and lead organizations, it is about the people and understanding them and motivating them.
turns.zh: 接下来要讨论的是领导力与执行力角色的差异，以及如何逐步过渡到领导角色。首先，当你把所有事情都做得很好，并掌握了所需的核心技能后，接下来你需要了解的是如何理解他人及其动机。在产品开发过程中，必须弄清楚用户为何会使用你的产品？他们要解决什么问题？为何会点击那个按钮？点击后能给他们带来怎样的愉悦感？又会让他们感到沮丧和不满？还有哪些行为是他们不想做的。因此，在产品开发和团队管理中，理解用户动机至关重要。比如用户为何要点击某个按钮？为何要加入你的团队？他们为何愿意努力工作？他们想达成什么目标？职业规划又如何？（00:06:54）：所以你必须善于解读他人，通过提问来深入理解他们的想法。我要分享一个对我很有帮助的例子——这听起来有点奇怪，但我父亲是一名心理医生。在成长过程中，每次家庭聚会或社交活动结束后，他总会分析现场情况，猜测他人的心理活动，比如某人为何会那样说话。这让我学会了观察整个场景，留意人们的反应。比如在开会时，当你说完某句话后，看看其他人的表情。只要用心观察，就能读懂很多东西。因此，想要为用户打造产品并领导团队，关键在于理解用户、激发他们的积极性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this advice. I feel like we could do a whole podcast on just this topic. So on this last point about understanding people, is there an example of this in either a product you built of just like, "Oh, here's something I noticed about someone using Slack or Google or Amazon that changed the way I think about building this specific feature."?
turns.zh: 我非常赞同这种建议。我觉得我们完全可以就这个话题做一期播客。回到理解用户的最后一点，你能否举个例子，比如在你开发的产品中，发现了某个用户使用Slack、Google或亚马逊时的行为，让你重新思考了某个功能的设计？

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: One of the things that I caution product managers about is that you don't want to be too overly reliant on metrics and you want to also have an intuition. You want product managers who understand intuitively their customers and their product and sometimes you'll make decisions because you just know it's the right thing to do because it feels right and it usually is right if you understand your product well enough. How do you get good at it? Ask a lot of questions. Don't assume you know. Marc Benioff would always say, "Have a beginner's mind. Go in assuming that you know nothing and listen to your customers, listen to the people." Because I also see this as you're building a feature and you think it's the best thing. Because of course everyone's going to want it because you worked on it and you're going to put it front and center in the interface where everybody's going to see it. Well, no, you got to earn that right. And that is another thing that people do is they want the thing they worked on to be right there, but it might not be the most important thing that a person needs at that point. So have perspective. Have perspective of what your users are actually trying to achieve.
turns.zh: 我要提醒产品经理的一点是，不要过度依赖数据指标，而是要培养直觉力。我们需要产品经理能直观理解用户和产品，有时你会基于直觉做出决策，因为你觉得这就是正确的选择。若你对产品足够了解，这种直觉通常是正确的。如何培养这种能力？多提问。不要想当然。马克·贝尼奥夫常说：“保持初学者的心态。假设自己一无所知，倾听用户和团队的声音。” 我也认为，在开发某个功能时，你可能认为它很棒，因为毕竟是你亲手打造的，还把它放在界面显眼位置让所有人看到。但不行，你必须赢得用户的认可。有些人急于把自己费心打造的东西推送出去，但这未必是用户当下最需要的。所以要保持客观，理解用户的真实需求。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Going back to your first point about doing a great job at the job you have, I imagine some people hear this and the advice is do a great job at the job you're already doing, and they may feel like they are, and there's other reasons they aren't being promoted. Is there an example from your career or a story you could tell of just like to clarify what doing a great job look like where it's not just like I hit my goals. It's like, here's what it looks like. Here's how you actually get ahead.
turns.zh: 回到你提到的第一点——在现有工作中做到出色。我想有些人听到这个建议时，会觉得自己已经在尽力了，但可能仍未获得晋升。这里能否举个职业生涯中的例子或故事，帮助我们更清晰地理解“出色表现”具体意味着什么？毕竟，仅仅达成目标并不够，还需要展现出推动业务发展的能力。

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: Are you helping the business move forward? So it's not about I achieve what I was asked to do, but did you build something that people actually used? It's not about just launching something and did you do the right thing for the company? And that is different. It's a different mindset. Did you enable the entire organization to be more productive despite you? I remember very early in my career I was working as an engineer and I was offered a job to manage a team that was across different programs. I took a vacation, I came back and I said, "I don't think this team should exist." It was my first management job and I wanted to be a manager. And I said, "Here's why I don't think that this team should exist. It's not the right thing for the company. It's not going to be productive." And my manager was so stunned. He was like, "Wait. You're saying no?" I'm like, "Yeah, because here's how you should organize it." And then he's like, "You're right, and I'll find you something else," and he did.
turns.zh: 你是否在助力企业向前发展？这不仅关乎完成既定任务，还要创造出真正被人们使用的产品。不仅仅是推出一项新服务，更要为公司做出正确决策。这两者有着本质区别，需要转变思维模式。比如，即便在你缺席的情况下，整个组织也能提高效率吗？我记得职业生涯早期，我担任工程师时，公司让我管理一个跨多个项目的团队。我休假归来后坦言：“我认为这个团队不该存在。” 那是我首次担任管理职位，但我渴望成为一名管理者。我说：“这个团队不该存在。这对公司没有益处，也无法提升效率。” 我的上司惊讶不已：“等等，你说不成立？” 我回答：“没错，因为应该这样调整架构。” 他说：“你说得对，我会给你另谋高就。” 后来他真的这么做了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If I were to put this into one word, it's impact. Drive impact.
turns.zh: 如果用一个词概括，那就是“影响力”。要创造影响力。

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Okay. Going in a different direction, we were chatting before we started recording this and something that you shared with me, and some people may be really surprised to hear this, but I completely agree with this take, is that you don't need to be a well-run business to win. I've seen this myself. I'd love to hear your insights here and especially where you notice this. What parts of your career noticed this to be true?
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，换个话题。录制前我们聊到，你曾分享过一个观点——有些人可能很惊讶，但我完全认同：企业无需完美运作也能取胜。我亲身见证过这种现象。能否分享你的见解，尤其是你职业生涯中遇到的具体案例？

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: I love working at well-run companies. It's more fun, your people are happier. I like running a well-run team, so I aspire to have a very well run team and to work at a well run company. But what I've seen is when a company isn't well run like IT isn't working, marketing is broken, there are not enough people in HR, there's a lot of turnover. All of these things I've seen that they're not correlated to the company being successful. So I can think of a couple examples right now of companies I know ... Not Glean, where I'm working today. Where there's high executive turnover. Where people get yelled at. There are lots of people fired. There's reorgs all the time. People I talk to are super unhappy, but the numbers are amazing. They're growing like crazy. And the opposite sit is also true. I can think of one company I know really well, amazing, CEO, well run, well oiled machine, everything. Hired good executives and they flat lined. (00:12:51): So you just see it. You see it over and over again and people get very upset about these things that aren't working. And one of the things that I try and do is give a perspective of what matters and what doesn't. And it might even be to the sales team because you get all these requests for features all the time. If you did every single one, it would be impossible. Even if you did, 80, 90% of them won't matter for the success of the company. But then there are some that really matter. So what are the things that really matter? We always talk about product market fit. Nobody really knows what product market fit is. Everybody has a different explanation, but it means people want to use your product. That they're clamoring for it. So you've built something that people value and that people value and that solves a problem for them, but that's also not good enough. You need to build a great product, but you also have to have distribution and you need to have a sales team that works. And you have to have enough money in the bank to get there. So those are probably the things that are the most important. I might be missing something. (00:13:58): And then within each of those, there's the things that really mattered and there's so many features that we built at Slack that were the most important features ever that failed and nobody used so it clearly didn't have an impact. And you can see that in retrospect, but I think after being at multiple different big companies and small companies, I have that perspective of let's just make sure that we do the right things and don't get too worked up about all the things that are broken because every startup has so many things that are broken.
turns.zh: 我喜欢在管理良好的公司工作。这里更具乐趣，员工也更快乐。我也喜欢管理一支高效运作的团队，因此我渴望能拥有一支管理出色的团队，并在一家运作良好的公司任职。但我所见过的很多公司管理不善——比如IT系统故障、市场营销失灵、人力资源部门人手不足、人员流动率高等——这些问题与公司的成功并无关联。举几个我熟悉的例子吧……比如我今天所在的Glean公司。那里高管流动率极高，员工经常被吼骂，很多人被解雇，组织架构调整频繁。虽然我交谈过的员工都非常不满，但公司的数据却惊人——他们增长速度惊人。反之亦然。我还能想到一家我非常熟悉的公司，CEO出色，管理有方，团队运转顺畅，但最终业绩却停滞不前。（00:12:51）你会发现这种现象反复出现，人们对这些问题困扰不已。我努力为人们提供一个正确的视角，告诉他们什么重要，什么不重要。这甚至适用于销售团队，因为他们总被要求添加各种功能特性。如果你满足每个需求，那根本不可能做到。即便你满足了80%、90%的需求，对公司的成功也毫无意义。但有些需求确实至关重要。那么哪些才是真正重要的呢？我们总在谈论“产品市场契合度”，但没人真正理解其含义。每个人的解释都不同，但其核心是人们愿意使用你的产品，迫切需求你的产品。这意味着你开发了有价值的产品，解决了用户痛点，但这还不够。你还需要打造优质产品，搭建有效的销售团队，并确保资金充足。这些才是最关键的要素。可能我还遗漏了某些关键点。（00:13:58）在这些要素中，又有一些真正重要的部分。比如Slack开发的许多最重要功能特性最终未能普及，显然对公司业绩毫无影响。回过头来看，你会发现这些教训。但在多家大公司和小公司任职后，我形成了这样一种观点：确保做正确的事，别为那些失控的混乱状况焦虑不已，因为每个初创公司都面临诸多亟待解决的难题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I think a really interesting insight here is that if you're working at a company that is just chaotic and it feels like we don't know what we're doing, I don't know how this thing is running, I don't know how this will continue to be successful, your experience is it ... Is it that most of the successful companies you've been at are just chaotic internally and aren't incredibly run and that's normal, that's very typical?
turns.zh: 所以我认为一个非常有趣的洞察是，如果你所在的公司混乱无序，感觉方向不明，运作不清，员工也无从知晓未来如何发展，那么你可能会发现，大多数你曾就职过的成功公司内部同样混乱，管理不善，这其实很正常、很典型。

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: Until they get to a certain scale. Now, once you reach a certain scale and you've already conquered the market, then you need to be well run. Then you bring in professional managers and things are about the cost and executing and getting all the ... Once you get to over 5,000 people or 10,000 people, you got to have things that ... Then you're a growth engine. You have to know what phase you're in and what's important at that phase. So it isn't that at every phase, chaos is okay, and also some chaos is okay and some chaos is not okay. If you're changing your strategy all the time and you're changing your direction and you're changing projects on people all the time so that they can't actually achieve anything ... So this is again, so you can't simplify it that some chaos is okay and some isn't. And also some chaos is right for you as a person. There are some really great companies I would never work at because they don't fit me. They're not a company I would enjoy going to work in the morning or they're not aligned with what I'm good at. So just because a company is doing well, if the chaos is chaos and something that's going to make you upset and unhappy don't work there.
turns.zh: 直到公司发展到一定规模。现在，一旦你达到了某个规模，并且已经征服了市场，那么你就需要高效运营。此时你会引入专业管理者，所有事务都围绕成本、执行力和项目推进展开。一旦员工规模超过5000人或10000人，你就必须建立完善的管理体系。然后，你会成为一个增长引擎。你必须清楚自己所处的阶段，以及该阶段的核心任务。因此，并非每个阶段都允许混乱存在——有些混乱是可控的，而有些则不然。如果你频繁调整战略、方向和项目，导致员工无法达成任何目标……所以不能简单地认为某些混乱是可以接受的，而有些则不行。此外，有些混乱对你个人而言是合适的。有些优秀的公司我绝不会加入，因为它们不适合我。它们不是那种能让我早上愉快上班的公司，也不符合我的才能。所以即便公司表现出色，但若混乱程度失控、令人不安、不快乐，那就别去了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a correlation there? Just like companies that have strong product market fit, things are just breaking as they're going through hyper growth? Just thoughts on why this is the case.
turns.zh: 这两者之间有联系吗？比如那些产品市场契合度高的公司，在高速增长期是否会频繁出现系统崩溃？我只是想探讨其中的原因。

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: A lot of it is that because if you are in hyper growth, you've got customers coming at a really fast pace, you're growing your company really quickly and the number of employees and it's just really hard to keep up. Because things in the infrastructure break, things in the communication breakdown. You've got at any given point 50% of the company has been there less than six months. But you have to grow really fast because once you hit product market fit, if you don't, then your growth will stop. So if you're suddenly growing, especially if you're an enterprise company, you have to have salespeople, if you're a consumer company or systems have to keep running as you scale. And look at companies like MySpace, well, they died because their product got too slow. And so some companies have initial product market fit and then they don't keep up. So I do think a lot of it is it's very hard to grow that fast. And so things really do start breaking, but then once you get all the right leadership in place, processes in place, then it starts to get better. So it goes through ups and downs in level of chaos.
turns.zh: 很大程度上是因为高速增长阶段，客户涌入速度极快，公司扩张迅速，员工数量激增，基础设施和沟通系统往往难以跟上节奏。公司可能有50%的员工入职不到六个月，但你必须快速发展，因为一旦产品市场契合度未达标，增长就会停滞。例如MySpace就因为产品速度过慢而倒闭。有些公司最初有产品市场契合度，但后续未能保持优势。因此，快速增长的难度极大，系统会频繁崩溃。但一旦引入合适的领导团队和流程，情况就会改善。因此，混乱程度会经历起起落落。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's one takeaway here that product market fit solves a lot of problems. Strong product market fit.
turns.zh: 有一个关键点是产品市场契合度能解决许多问题。强大的产品市场契合度至关重要。

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: Well, no product market fit is a death sentence. I would say it more like that. If you built a product that people aren't really excited to use, then you don't have a company because it's very hard to do that unless you have distribution machine and then you catch up over time. But we will not name companies like that. So there are other ways of doing it, but yeah, that is the most important thing.
turns.zh: 嗯，没有产品市场契合度就是死刑判决。我更愿意这么说。若你开发的产品用户不愿使用，那公司就没戏了，除非有强大的分销渠道并逐步改进。但我们不会点名批评那些公司。当然也有其他成功之道，但产品市场契合度确实是最关键的因素。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I will say during my experience at Airbnb, I absolutely saw this. It was just nonstop chaos. And I always felt like, well, how is this continuing to operate and succeed? Things are just out of control. Everything's changing every six months. I don't know what's happening here. And I think a lesson here is just that's normal for a hyper growth business that has strong product market fit. But again, not a good excuse to just allow chaos. And it's not like chaos means success, right?
turns.zh: 是啊。在Airbnb的经历中，我确实亲眼目睹了这种情况。简直是无休止的混乱。我总在想，嗯，这家公司怎么还能持续运营并取得成功呢？一切都失控了。每六个月就换个新玩法。我真搞不明白这里的逻辑。我觉得一个教训就是，这对一个产品市场高度契合、增长超快的公司来说，是再正常不过的了。但即便如此，也不能把混乱当作借口。毕竟混乱不等于成功，对吧？

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: And it's not a good excuse to not have an organization that's functioning. You should still strive to have an organization that's functioning and keep people happy and motivated and all that.
turns.zh: 同样，不能以组织混乱为借口。你还是应该努力建立一个高效运转的组织，让员工开心、充满动力之类的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Great. Okay. Another maybe contrarian opinion that you hold along the career track is that you don't need to plan your career. I also 100% agree with this. I had no plan for my career. I never knew where the hell I was going to go. I never had this vision of here's what I want to do. I just followed things that were pulling me and things that seemed interesting. I love that you also tell people this. I'd love to hear your insights here. Especially for someone that's either struggling with their career or just stressed. They don't have a plan or their plan's not working the way they wanted it to.
turns.zh: 不错。好的。关于职业发展，你还有个可能与众不同的观点——你认为没必要规划职业生涯。我完全赞同这一点。我从不规划职业生涯，从不知道自己要去哪儿，也从未设想过自己想做什么。我只是顺着那些吸引我、看起来有趣的事物前进。我很欣赏你能把这种理念传递给别人。能听听你的见解吗？尤其是对那些正为职业发展苦苦挣扎，或者倍感压力的人——他们没有规划，或者现有规划效果不理想。

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: Really recently I was talking to somebody in their twenties who was asking me for career advice. Should I be a product manager, et cetera. And I'm trying to put together my five-year plan and I said, "I never had a five-year plan." So to be clear, some people need that. That's the kind of people they are. They want the planning. I said, "It's great if you want that, but I never had it." And the person I was talking to just relaxed and they're like, "Oh my God, that's so great to hear because I have no idea what I want to do in five years." I'm like, "I still have no idea what I want to do in five years. I've never had an idea what I want to do in five years." Early in your career you have a lot more angst about it because the forks in the road are more significant because they can go, do I go get an MBA or do I go work for somebody? Do I be a product manager or an engineer? And those really take you in very different paths. (00:20:09): And I meet a lot of kids in their ... I shouldn't call them kids. My kids are my kids' friends. But a lot of people who are younger in their career who are struggling with this a little bit. So what I believe, and I've always believed is that you follow people. You learn the most from people. I don't look for domains. Some people have a domain, like I'm super interested in climate or whatever and they really want to work in that area and that's fine so maybe within that area. But you follow people who are the best at what they do. So it's not good enough to follow somebody who you like. You want to follow somebody who's either the best product thinker or the best engineer or the best salesperson. And so that you will learn the skill of how to be the best at that. (00:21:01): So you follow people where you're going to learn the most. And a way to do that also is you look at where the great people are going. So you want to go to companies where there's also a nexus of great people because they together will do great things. And even if the company fails or succeeds, but not as much as you'd like, you still have those connections. Everybody talks about the PayPal Mafia and how they've gone on to do things. I was super lucky to be at Google for so many years and I spent a lot of time with Googlers that I met and that are all working in different companies now because you build those relationships by working together. So if you follow people and where you're going to learn the most and you go step by step, I think that's a great way of progressing in your career.
turns.zh:
最近我和一位二十多岁的年轻人聊天，聊到职业规划，他问我：“我该不该做产品经理之类的？”我正努力制定自己的五年计划，就说了句：“我从没制定过五年计划。”说实话，有些人需要这种规划，他们就是这样的人——他们需要规划。我说：“如果你想这样做当然很好，但我从未这样过。”对方听后放松下来，说：“天哪，听到你这么说真是太棒了，因为我完全不知道五年后要做什么。”我又说：“我现在还是不知道五年后要做什么。我从未想过五年后要做什么。”  
在职业生涯早期，你会对此感到焦虑得多，因为人生路口更重大——比如是去读MBA还是直接工作，是做产品经理还是工程师。这些选择会把你引向截然不同的道路。（00:20:09）我遇到很多年轻人，特别是刚入行不久的人，他们正为此纠结。我一直坚信的一点是，跟随优秀的人学习。学习最快的方式就是向他人请教。我不追逐特定领域。有些人有专注的领域，比如气候变化之类的，他们特别想在那个领域工作，这没问题。但你要追随最擅长本职的人——无论是产品策划大师、顶级工程师还是销售高手，这样你才能掌握他们的技能。（00:21:01）所以要去能学到最多知识的地方。找到优秀人才聚集的公司也很重要，因为他们能共同创造奇迹。即便公司失败或未达预期，你也能收获人脉。大家都听说过“PayPal黑手党”（指PayPal前员工后来创立的公司），他们后来成就非凡。我曾在谷歌工作多年，与许多谷歌人保持联系，他们如今分散在不同公司，但共同的经历让联系永久。追随能教会你最多的人，脚踏实地前行，我认为这是职业发展的最佳路径。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's such tactical advice. And I've seen this work for a lot of people that just go where their favorite former employees work. And not favorite to your point, but the people that they most respect and have been most impressed by. And I think it's such an easy thing to do. It's a really easy heuristic for understanding where to go. There's something Marc Andreessen once shared that I'm reminded of when you say this. There's a term for this, I forget the actual term, but there's certain companies have this gravitational pull where they are acquiring all the best talent. They're currently the gravity in the space and everyone awesome is going there. And you have to, as a company, know you're one of those companies or you're the opposite. You're losing all the people and they're all going to this other company. I guess any thoughts on that?
turns.zh: 这真是些实用的建议。我见过很多人，他们会去前雇主最青睐的公司工作。不一定是特别喜欢前雇主，而是最尊敬、最钦佩的人。这样做其实很简单，是个理解职业方向的简单启发。马克·安德森（Marc Andreessen）曾提到过一个概念，当你谈到这个时，我突然想起他。有一个术语，具体叫什么我记不清了，但有些公司有种引力效应，能吸引最优秀的人才。他们是所在领域的引力中心，所有杰出人才都会汇聚于此。作为公司，你要么成为这样的引力中心，要么相反——失去人才，人才都流向其他公司。对此你有什么看法吗？

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: Yeah. And it's really bad when you don't have a gravitational pull. It's super hard. I would say that one thing that if you're a manager, I always advise managers, go somewhere where you can recruit. I got a piece of advice from a friend that I thought was amazing advice as a leader. She said to me, "Take a job where if you hire people, it's going to make their careers." I was like, "Whoa." Because I was getting offers for some turnaround jobs. And if you think you can turn around, great. But if you're going to hire the best people, you want to make sure that it's going to be a good place for them and that they're going to learn and they're going to grow. And so you want to do right by them. And you really earnestly want to say you can make your career by coming here. (00:23:36): And I thought that gave such a higher bar for every job I was looking at as a leader that I thought it was just amazing advice. And then on the flip side, on the negative side, some people are putting too much emphasis on where will I get a big financial return? And I've found that financial returns are the hardest to predict. You know who's good. You know who you want to work with. You can predict where you're going to learn. Because even if a company fails, you learn a lot. But predicting financial success is so hard because you don't know what's going to happen with the market, with the world, with crypto, and Meta AI. And people who do that and say ... I had one person say, "I took this job because I'm a mercenary. They just paid me a ton." Did not work out for him. And I feel really bad when people do that, but I think that it's a dangerous thing to do.
turns.zh: 是啊。当你没有引力作用时，情况就很糟糕了。这真的太难了。我要说的是，如果你是一位管理者，我总是建议他们去能招募人才的地方。我从一位朋友那里得到了一条我认为作为领导者非常棒的建议。她对我说：“找一份能让招聘的人成就事业的工作。”我当时就惊到了，因为我当时接到了一些扭转局面的工作的邀约。当然，如果你觉得自己能扭转局面，那很棒。但如果你要招募最优秀的人才，就得确保那里对他们来说是个好去处，让他们能学习和成长。所以你得对他们负责，真心实意地说来这里就能成就他们的事业。（00:23:36）我觉得这为我作为领导者审视每一份工作设定了更高的标准，简直太棒了。而另一方面，负面的情况是，有些人过于看重能获得多大的经济回报。我发现经济回报是最难预测的。你知道谁很优秀，你知道想和谁共事，你能预测能在哪里学习。但预测经济成功太难了，因为你不知道市场、世界、加密货币和元AI会如何变化。那些这样做的人最后结果都不好。我对此真的很心疼，但我认为这是一件危险的事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I imagine some people hearing this advice are going to feel like, "I'm not going to get a job at OpenAI or Glean or other awesome companies that everyone wants to go work at." Any advice to those folks?
turns.zh: 我想有些听了这个建议的人可能会觉得：“我又不是能去OpenAI、Glean或其他所有人想去工作的超棒公司工作。”对这些人有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: There's lots of good companies and there's lots of smart people. You don't have to be at the top brand. And if you go somewhere where you're going to learn and it's going to get you there. I made mistakes. I went to some companies, multiple companies that failed or stopped growing and didn't do well or didn't have all the right people. Careers you don't make every step is to the right place. You remember in what you cited, all the companies I went to that did well, you left out all the ones that I went to that didn't do well. And so then people will assume that every time I made a job change, it was to a company that did well. No. That was not the case. So if you focus on that learning bit, you will get there. And there are lots of paths. There isn't just the OpenAI or Glean or Anthropic.
turns.zh: 有很多好公司，也有很多人才。你不必非得在顶级品牌工作。只要去能让你学习、能助你成功的地方就行。我也犯过错。我去过很多公司，失败的或停止增长的公司，不成功的公司，或者没有合适人才的公司。职业生涯不是每一步都能选对地方。你记得你提到的那些我去过且成功的公司，却没提到那些不成功的公司。所以人们会以为每次换工作都是去成功的公司。不是这样的。所以如果你专注于学习这部分，你就能成功。路径有很多，不只有OpenAI、Glean或Anthropic。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. And again, I love how tactical this is. If someone is trying to figure out where to go work if they're unhappy in their current job or don't have a job right now is just make a list of the people you most respect that are the best at the thing they do, see where they work and there's your list of companies to potentially go after. There's a lot of benefits to this as you shared. It's not just helping you pick the place to work, it's the network. It'll level you up. Is there anything else along those lines that is helpful for people to think about why this is a really good strategy?
turns.zh: 太棒了。再说一次，我喜欢这种切实可行的方法。如果有人想弄清楚如果对当前工作不满或目前失业该去哪里工作，就列出你最尊敬的、在各自领域最出色的人，看看他们在哪里工作，这就是潜在的目标公司名单。正如你所分享的，这有很多好处。这不仅能帮你选择工作地点，还能拓展人脉，让你提升自己。还有其他类似的建议能帮助人们理解为什么这是一个非常好的策略吗？

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: Skills can't be taken away. A company can fail, but if you learn a skill, you will always have that skill.
turns.zh: 技能是永远不会被剥夺的。一家公司可能会倒闭，但如果你掌握了一项技能，你将永远拥有它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. And I've totally seen this to work, so I really love that you're focusing on this advice. You've mentioned places you've worked and folks you've worked with. You worked with folks like Jeff Bezos, Stewart Butterfield, some of the top product thinkers, leaders in the world. So let me just ask, what's one thing you learned from Jeff Bezos and Stewart Butterfield?
turns.zh: 我特别赞同这一观点。我也亲眼见证过它行之有效，所以我很欣赏你对这条建议的关注。你提到了曾工作过的公司和共事过的同事。比如杰夫·贝索斯、斯图尔特·巴特菲尔德等全球顶尖的产品设计师和行业领袖。那么我想问，你从杰夫·贝索斯和斯图尔特·巴特菲尔德身上学到了哪些东西？

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: Probably can't narrow it down to one, but I'll talk about Bezos first. I was very lucky to join Amazon early when I still ... I had quarterly meetings with Jeff Bezos. And this was before AWS launched, so it was before Amazon was known in the Valley. This is another example. I went there because I went to work for Udi Manbe who started A9 and he was talking to me one night trying to recruit me and he spent two hours on the phone with me telling me how amazing Jeff Bezos was. And this was before there were any books on him. And that really convinced me to go there. So there's a lot written on Bezos. Read his shareholder letters, read the books about him, read Colin Bryar's Working Backwards. The Everything Box I think it's called or The Everything Store.
turns.zh: 可能很难只归结为一点，但我先谈谈贝索斯。我很幸运能在亚马逊早期加入，当时我……每季度都会和杰夫·贝索斯开会。当时AWS还没推出呢，亚马逊在硅谷还不算知名。这又是一个例子。我之所以去亚马逊，是因为我要去为Udi Manbe工作，他是A9的创始人。有一天晚上，他想招我去工作，花了两个小时跟我聊杰夫·贝索斯有多了不起。当时还没有关于贝索斯的书呢。这真的说服了我，让我下定决心去亚马逊。关于贝索斯的书很多，可以读他的股东信，读关于他的书，比如Colin Bryar的《Working Backwards》，还有《The Everything Store》。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The Everything Store. Yeah.
turns.zh: 《The Everything Store》。对。

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: There's so many good books and there's so much to learn about how he works. So I won't try and cover those things. The things that stood out to me from the meetings I had with him were a couple of things. One, a lot of people have written about these six pagers, so he doesn't believe in PowerPoint. You write a six pager about ... It's like studying for the final exam is writing these six pagers. So you go into the meeting and there's the people around the table, his executive team and him. First he does not speak until everybody around the table speaks. So he goes around to all his leads and said, "What do you think? What do you think? What do you think?" And I'm sitting there like, "I don't care what anyone think. I just want to hear what Bezos thinks." But he wants to make sure that it's a team effort and that he's listening to what everybody in his organization thinks. (00:28:17): And he always spoke last. He is by far the smartest person I've ever met in my life. I've worked with a lot of smart people. But his ability to go deep in any domain and nail the core issue, and remember. We would've quarterly meetings and from quarter to quarter he would remember things that he had talked about before and then he would go into the architecture of search and why are you doing it this way or that way? And you're just blown away that he knows that. For me, the biggest takeaway from those meetings was his consistency, which is he had principles that it made it easier for you to operate in his company because you knew what he cared about because he always had these principles. Everything had to be customer driven, everything had to be relevant for the customer. (00:29:12): He hated icons. That was just the thing. You had to write what they were because people couldn't figure out what they are. So anytime you showed an icon, he would get annoyed. But you would go in and after a couple of meetings you're like, "Okay. I know what he's going to ask about. I know how he's thinking and I know what his principles are." And I think that consistency enables you to operate a large organization more effectively. And then there's one other thing that I really remember was one of the few really small meetings I was in with him and we were presenting working on a new product, and I was like, "Our competitors have 10 times as many people as we do on this." And he looks at me and he said, "That is your advantage." And then he goes into his talk about how it's a hill and it takes seven years to build a product. You can't look at it in the near term. You have to be in it for the long term. You can be sure I never went in and said, "I need a lot more resources." So that was Bezos.
turns.zh: 好书太多了，关于他如何运作的学习资料也数不胜数。所以我就不打算一一展开讲解了。在与他会面时，有几件事让我印象深刻。首先，很多人都写过关于“六页文档”的文章，所以他不喜欢用PowerPoint。写六页文档就好比为期末考试做准备。所以开会时，会议桌旁围坐着他的高管团队和他本人。他会先让在座的每个人发言，直到所有人都发完言后，他才开口。于是他挨个询问手下负责人，“你怎么看？你怎么看？你怎么看？”我坐在那里想，“我才不在乎别人怎么想，我只想听贝索斯怎么说。”但他希望确保这是团队的共同努力，所以会认真倾听组织内每个人的意见。（00:28:17）他总是在最后发言。他是我这辈子见过最聪明的人。我合作过很多聪明的人，但贝索斯在任何领域都能深入研究核心问题并牢记于心，这让我惊叹不已。我们每季度开会时，他总能记得之前讨论过的内容，然后深入探讨搜索架构，追问为什么要这样设计而不是那样设计。他的专业素养令人敬佩。对我而言，这些会议最大的收获在于他的始终如一——他秉持一系列原则，让你在他的公司里更容易开展工作，因为你清楚他的关注点所在。一切都要以客户为导向，一切都要与客户相关。（00:29:12）他讨厌图标。就是这样。你必须把图标解释清楚，否则人们根本看不明白。所以每次展示图标时，他都会很不耐烦。但参加几次会议后，你就会领悟到他的思考方式，明白他的原则所在。我认为这种一以贯之的作风能更高效地运营一家大型组织。还有一件事让我印象深刻，那次是我与他参加的为数不多的小型会议之一。我们展示一个新产品时，我说：“我们的竞争对手在这方面投入的人力是我们的十倍。”他看着我说：“这正是你的优势所在。” 然后他开始谈论如何将产品视为一座山峰，花七年时间打造产品，不能只看短期效益，必须着眼长远。我可以肯定，我再也不会去要求“我需要更多资源”了。这就是贝索斯。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: Stewart. Again, I went to Slack because I wanted to work with Stewart Butterfield. I think he is the best product thinker in the Valley. He's not working in product right now. He's taking time off. But he's got this combination of long-term thinking and in the details. So in 2014, he wrote a master plan for Slack, which was build a product people love, build a network. That's Slack Connect. Build a platform that makes all of your other SaaS products more valuable. That's Slack Platform. And then do some magic AI stuff. Magic AI stuff took a lot longer, but-
turns.zh: 斯图尔特。再说一次，我加入Slack是因为我想与斯图尔特·巴特菲尔德共事。我认为他是硅谷最出色的产品设计师。他现在不负责产品工作了，正在休假。但他兼具长远思考和注重细节的能力。所以2014年，他为Slack制定了一个宏伟计划：打造人们喜爱的产品，搭建社交网络（即Slack Connect），打造让其他SaaS产品更具价值的平台（即Slack Platform），然后开发一些神奇的AI技术。虽然AI技术花费了更长时间，但——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That was part of his plan early on is magic AI stuff.
turns.zh: 这正是他早期计划中的一部分——开发神奇的AI技术。

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: It literally was. There was a grid with four boxes in 2014 and it never changed. That was his master plan and what we worked on each year changed. But somebody recently asked me, "You guys did Slack Connect much later?" I'm like, "Yeah, but it was always part of the plan." It was always part of his vision. So he saw forward in the vision, but he also was very much into the details. And I think the thing that I learned from him the most was the power of prototyping. And that even though he was such a great product thinker, he would always say, "I can't tell you if this is going to work. I have to feel it. I have to try it. And a mock-up doesn't tell you what it's going to feel like." And he would push people to do prototypes, not incremental of just to get a feature out, but really to think. Very soon after I started, we launched ... I hired a design lead, Ethan Eismannn, and he led a redesign of the new information architecture for Slack.
turns.zh: 确实如此。2014年的时候，我们的界面有四个模块框架，从那以后就再没改过。这一直是他的宏伟蓝图，也是我们每年努力的方向。但最近有人问我：“你们为什么这么晚才推出Slack Connect？”我回答：“是啊，但这始终是计划的一部分。” 这始终是他的愿景。他能预见未来，但又对细节一丝不苟。我从他身上学到最重要的一点就是原型设计的力量。尽管他是如此出色的产品设计师，但他总会说：“我没法预测这是否可行。我必须亲身感受，亲自尝试。模型永远无法还原真实体验。” 他会敦促团队制作原型，不只是为了快速上线某个功能，更是为了深度思考。在我加入不久后，我们就推出了……我聘请了设计主管Ethan Eismannn，他主导了Slack新信息架构的重新设计。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I worked with Ethan at Airbnb.
turns.zh: 我曾在Airbnb与Ethan共事。

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: Oh yeah.
turns.zh: 哦，对啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: He was head of design for the search experience and the search team.
turns.zh: 他曾担任搜索体验和搜索团队的设计主管。

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: Yeah. Ethan is awesome. And he came in and his first task was to work with Stewart on this redesign. And Stewart came in and said, "I want you to take everything in the interface and put it behind one button." And everyone's like, "That's never going to work." And he's like, "Do it. Just do it." And so we had our prototypers ... We had also engineers, front-end engineers who were really good at prototyping, literally took everything in the interface and put it behind one button and he said, "This is how you're going to see what you really need in the interface." So we were never going to ship that, but it was the beginning of the redesign.
turns.zh: 是的。Ethan非常棒。他加入团队后，首要任务就是与Stewart合作重新设计界面。当Stewart提出“把界面上的所有元素都整合到一个按钮后面”时，所有人都说：“这根本行不通。”他却说：“就这么做。放手去做。” 于是我们的原型设计师……还有前端工程师，他们都非常擅长原型设计，真的把界面上的所有元素都整合到一个按钮后面。他说：“这就是你能发现界面中真正需要的功能的方式。” 虽然我们最终没能正式发布这个设计，但这正是重新设计的开端。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let me tell you about a product called Sidebar. The most successful people that I know surround themselves with incredible peers. When you have a trusted group of peers, you can discuss challenges you're having, get career advice and just gut check how you're thinking about your work, your career and your life. This gives you more than a leg up. It gives you a leap forward. Having a group of trusted and amazing peers was key to my career growth. And this is the Sidebar ethos, but it's hard to build this trusted group of peers on your own. Sidebar is a platform for senior tech professionals, director to C-level to advance in their career. Members are matched into peer groups to lean on for unbiased opinions, diverse perspectives and raw feedback. Guided by world-class programming and facilitation, all running on Sidebar's technology Sidebar enables you to get focused tactical feedback at every step of your career journey. (00:33:35): If you're a listener of this podcast, you're already committed to growth. Sidebar is the missing piece to catalyze your career. 93% of members say Sidebar helped them achieve a significant positive change in their career. Check them out at sidebar.com/lenny. (00:33:52): As a product leader, how do you think about just the time it takes to create a prototype in something like this? As a pm I'm just like a lot of times we don't have time to build this whole prototype. We got to ship stuff, we got to hit these calls, we got experiments to run, we'll just build it and see how it goes. How do you think about making time for something like that?
turns.zh: 让我跟你讲讲Sidebar这个产品。我认识的最成功的人都会围绕自己身边汇聚一群优秀的同行。当你拥有一群值得信赖的同行时，你可以讨论遇到的挑战，获得职业建议，还能直击自己对工作、职业和生活的真实想法。这不仅仅是锦上添花，而是质的飞跃。拥有一群值得信赖且才华横溢的同行是职业成长的关键。这就是Sidebar的理念，但独自建立这样一个可靠的同行群体并非易事。Sidebar是一个面向高级科技专业人士（从总监到C级高管）的职业发展平台。成员会被匹配到同行小组，获取无偏见的意见、多元视角和真实反馈。在世界级编程和引导的支持下，所有功能都在Sidebar的技术平台上运行，让你能在职业生涯的每一步都获得专注的战术反馈。（00:33:35）：如果你听这个播客，就说明你已经致力于成长了。Sidebar正是催化你职业发展的缺失环节。93%的会员表示Sidebar帮助他们实现了职业生涯的显著积极变化。请访问sidebar.com/lenny了解详情。（00:33:52）：作为产品负责人，您如何看待为这类项目创建原型所需的时间？作为产品经理，很多时候我们没有时间搭建整个原型。我们必须上线产品，参加会议，进行实验，然后看看效果如何。您如何为这类事情腾出时间？

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: If you're doing it right, it'll be faster and you need to have an engineering infrastructure that enables prototyping. So some engineering infrastructures are too heavy and they don't actually enable prototyping. We had a problem with our mobile apps that it was too hard to prototype and we actually redesigned our mobile apps until we got to the point where it was easier because our desktop app was pretty easy to prototype. But you have to have a layer of abstraction that enables you to do that, and you have to have engineers who have a prototyping mindset, and if you build multiple things and you have this mindset as I'm willing to throw it away, you write code that is never going to make it to production so you can just crank it out much faster and then you can see what works and then you build the production code. Until you actually get to your end goal of something working faster. (00:35:02): But you need the engineering team to have the same mindset. The product and engineering have to work together and design because design is just in it. Sometimes you can get design engineers who are doing the prototyping. So your first prototypes are like Figma prototypes, and then you get prototypes on real data. When I was at Google, one of our teams, a front-end team, I remember we hired a bunch of prototypers and our head of front-end engineering said to me one day, this is my secret weapon. This is how we move faster. So I do think it's a mindset shift and a tech stack shift.
turns.zh: 如果你做得对，速度会更快，而且你需要拥有支持原型设计的工程基础设施。然而，有些工程基础设施过于复杂，实际上并不能实现原型设计。我们曾遇到过移动应用原型设计困难的问题，最终重新设计了移动应用，直到达到更易于原型设计的程度，因为我们的桌面应用原型设计相对容易。但你必须具备支持原型设计的抽象层，还要有具备原型设计思维的工程师。如果你构建多个版本，并秉持“随时可以放弃”的心态，就能更快地编写出永远不会投入生产的代码，然后快速验证效果，再构建最终的生产代码。最终才能真正实现更快的开发目标。（00:35:02）：但工程团队也需要有相同的思维模式。产品和工程团队必须协同设计，因为设计思维无处不在。有时你会让设计工程师负责原型设计。最初的原型可能是Figma上的线框图，之后会基于真实数据进行迭代。在谷歌时，我记得我们有一个前端团队，雇佣了一批原型设计师。有一天前端工程负责人对我说，这是我们的秘密武器。这就是我们加速进程的秘诀。所以我认为这既是思维模式的转变，也是技术栈的变革。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We're going to talk about AI later, but it's also getting easier to build prototypes with AI. There's this video recently that went around on Twitter where an eight-year-old girl was building an app and in like 45 minutes, she built a chatbot using this product called Cursor. So I think that'll unlock a lot of great product on opportunities and just accelerate this sort of work. I asked about Jeff Bezos and Stewart Butterfield. I'm curious if there's another leader you've worked with that maybe is less known that you also learned a ton from that might be worth talking about.
turns.zh: 我们稍后会谈论AI，但借助AI构建原型也变得越来越容易。最近Twitter上有个视频很火，一位8岁女孩用Cursor这样的产品在45分钟内开发出聊天机器人。我认为这将释放大量优秀的产品机会，并加速相关工作进程。我曾问及杰夫·贝索斯和斯图尔特·巴特菲尔德。很好奇是否还有其他不那么出名的领导者，你们也从他们身上学到很多，值得一谈。

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: I think that there are people who are really, really good at what they do. So Marc Benioff is an amazing marketeer. His marketing mind ... After the acquisition, I got the opportunity to onstage with him at Dreamforce for ... Because Slack was a new shiny thing so of course Slack was going to be in the keynote. And so I was in the Benioff's keynote two years in a row. And so I watched how he approaches his keynote and the whole thing around Dreamforce. Dreamforce is incredible at the impact that it has on the ecosystem. And so I think that as a product, people don't think of him as much, but as his marketing abilities are amazing what he's done.
turns.zh: 我认为有些人在各自领域确实非常出色。马克·贝尼奥夫就是一位杰出的营销大师。他的营销思维……收购完成后，我有机会在Dreamforce大会上与他同台……因为Slack当时是新晋的热门产品，所以Slack自然会成为主题演讲的焦点。因此，我连续两年登上贝尼奥夫的主题演讲舞台。我观察了他如何策划主题演讲，以及Dreamforce大会对整个生态系统的影响。作为产品经理，人们可能不太关注贝尼奥夫，但他的营销能力确实令人惊叹。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I've written posts about how various companies got started in Salesforce history. Always comes to mind where they go to conferences where's there's no software mascot walking around. And I remember they did something around one of their competitors where they just created some real controversy around someone.
turns.zh: 我曾写过多篇关于Salesforce历史上不同公司如何起步的文章。总是会想到那些参加会议却没有软件吉祥物四处宣传的场景。我记得他们针对竞争对手采取了某些行动，引发了不小的争议。

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: Well, they went into their competitor's conference and stood outside their competitor's conference.
turns.zh: 嗯，他们去了竞争对手的会议，并站在会议场地外。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Mm-hmm. Right. That's what it was.
turns.zh: 嗯。没错。就是这样。

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: This is in the Beyond Software. This is in his book that he wrote about the early phases of Salesforce. And it takes his guts. He pushes the envelope.
turns.zh: 这段内容出自《Beyond Software》一书，源自他关于Salesforce早期阶段的著作。需要勇气去突破常规，挑战极限。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. It's a really good point that people don't think of Marc Benioff as a marketer. And that's interesting that that's maybe the main thing you took away from him is just the power of marketing and the skill.
turns.zh: 我很欣赏这一点——人们通常不把马克·贝尼奥夫视为营销高手。这很有趣，或许你从他身上领悟到的最重要的东西，就是营销的力量和技巧。

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: He approaches his marketing presentations like a product person approaches their building their product.
turns.zh: 他做营销演示的方式，就如同产品经理打造产品时的心态。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Okay. Speaking of former colleagues, I asked one of your former colleagues, his name is Fuzzy Khos. He's now the CTO of Notion. You worked with him, I believe at Slack.
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，说到前同事，我采访了你的前同事——富齐·科斯。他现在是Notion的首席技术官。我记得你和他曾在Slack共事。

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: And at Google.
turns.zh: 还有谷歌。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And at Google. Wow. Okay. So I asked him what to ask you, and he said that you're amazing at building strong cross-functional relationships, especially with engineers. I know you used to be an engineer, so I get where that skill come from. What can you teach people about building stronger cross-functional relationships, especially PMs to build better relationships with their engineers, designers, other folks on their team?
turns.zh: 谷歌。哇哦。好的，我问他应该向你提什么问题，他说你特别擅长建立强大的跨职能合作关系，尤其是与工程师团队。他知道你曾是工程师，所以能理解这种技能的来源。关于如何建立更紧密的跨职能合作关系，尤其是让产品经理与工程师、设计师及团队其他成员建立更好的合作关系，你能给出哪些建议？

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: Probably the most important thing that a product leader does because if you have great ideas of what to build, but you can't get them built, then you go nowhere. So one, make sure somewhere where you have a good engineering partner. So Henderson was the co-founder and CTO of Slack, and I couldn't have asked for a better engineering partner. He's just awesome. And that has to be part of your evaluation criteria that you meet and value your engineering partner before you join or you know that it's not the right one and the organization is willing to make a change. So that can happen too. You can go in and understand that something has to change, but that is a very, very important thing of what you're doing and what you're assessing when you go in. And then I think what's really important is that you're aligned. You understand your roles and responsibilities and where you're going to divide and conquer and where you're going to be aligned. (00:39:29): You don't want any of this ... People in the organization, they asked Mom, they asked dad and they got different opinions and playing one against the other, that doesn't work. So one, you have to know that you're not going to do that. So if somebody would ask me something that it was in Cal's domain, I'd be like, "Did you talk to Cal?" I would never try and go around him. So we were very clear on, you're going to drive this, I'm going to drive this. And if it was unclear, we'd talk and we would say, "Okay. Who's going to take this one?" And we would do all our reviews together. And so all of the OKR reviews, we had weekly exec reviews, we had the updates on our OKRs, so we did them all together, but I knew here's the things that he was going to ask the questions on and dig deep. And then when I was, he would take a back seat, but of course we could ask questions in each other things, but I knew that he was taking ownership and he knew what I was taking ownership of. (00:40:24): But I think the bottom line was respect. Is that you have to respect and trust that they actually will follow up on what they say they will. In Cal and Fuzzy were amazing at that. I would go to Fuzzy and be like, "Hey, we need more mobile engineers because this one product is not going to ship." And he's like, "I'm on it. Got it." And that was all I needed to do. And obviously if he couldn't do it, he'd come back to me and, "Hey, there's going to be a problem." But it was like just things got done. That's the best part of it.
turns.zh: 或许产品负责人最重要的工作就是，如果你有绝佳的开发创意，但却无法将其付诸实践，那么你注定一事无成。因此，首先要确保你能找到一位优秀的工程合作伙伴。亨德森曾是Slack的联合创始人兼首席技术官，我找不到比他更出色的工程伙伴了。他简直太棒了。这必须成为你的评估标准之一——在加入团队前，你必须先了解并重视你的工程合作伙伴，否则你就会发现这并非理想的合作伙伴，组织也愿意做出调整。这种情况也时有发生。你可能进入新团队后发现某些问题需要改变，但这正是你评估时必须关注的关键点。然后，保持团队协同至关重要。你要明确各自的角色与职责，清楚如何分工协作、如何保持一致。（00:39:29）你绝不能让团队成员各自为政。比如，组织内有人向某位成员咨询某项决策，却得到不同的意见，进而相互拆台，这种做法注定行不通。因此，你必须坚守底线——如果有人向我咨询属于卡尔职责范围的事务，我会问：“你跟卡尔谈过了吗？”我绝不会越俎代庖。我们从一开始就明确分工：“你负责这个项目，我负责那个项目。”若有不确定的地方，我们会共同商议：“好吧，这项任务由谁来负责？”所有OKR评估都会同步进行，每周召开高管评审会，共同审议OKR进展。但我深知，卡尔会深度参与那些属于他的职责范畴，而我也会专注于自己的职责。（00:40:24）但最重要的原则是相互尊重。要相信对方会切实履行承诺。卡尔和富齐在这方面堪称典范。我会找到富齐，说：“嘿，我们需要更多移动端工程师，因为这个产品无法按时上线。”他会说：“我这就去办。”这就是我需要做的全部。显然，如果他无法完成任务，就会及时向我汇报：“嘿，出现问题了。”但最终任务总能完成。这正是最棒的地方。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You talked about being aligned, which I love and I fully have seen that power of that of you and your engine manager, design manager being aligned on ... And you tell me if I'm wrong, but specifically on what goals you're trying to achieve, what success looks like, things like that. Are there any tactics you found to create that alignment? And also if there's anything else you want to add to the point I just made about what it is you're specifically aligned on, that'd be great.
turns.zh: 你谈到了保持团队协同，这一点我深有共鸣，也充分见证了你与工程经理、设计经理在目标一致性方面的巨大力量……如果你觉得我理解有误，请纠正我。但具体来说，你们是如何在目标达成、成功定义等关键问题上保持一致的？有没有什么策略能有效促进这种协同？如果对上述协同要点有补充说明，那就再好不过了。

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: One, you got to spend a lot of time together. There isn't a way around that. And you have to document things and make sure that you've talked it through. And if you don't agree with something and you're not sure it's a priority, you have to speak up and you can't just be like, "Okay, whatever.", and then go to somebody in your team and be like, "Oh God, that that CTO, why did he make this decision?" That just doesn't work. So I'm a very direct person. So if I don't think that something is the right priority or is working, I will be very clear. We had different forms, so I'll be very tactical here on the forms that Cal and I had together.
turns.zh: 首先，你们得花大量时间在一起。这是无法避免的。你们必须把事情记录下来，并确保充分沟通。如果你对某件事有异议，或者不确定它是否是优先事项，你就得直言不讳，不能只是说“好吧，随便吧”，然后去找团队里的其他人抱怨：“天哪，那个CTO为什么要做这个决定？”这种做法根本行不通。所以我是个很直接的人。如果我觉得某件事不是正确的优先事项，或者没有效果，我会直言不讳。我们用OKR来推动流程，团队会向我们汇报OKR。当团队规模过大时，逐一审查每个团队的OKR太耗时了，所以我们为每个团队开设了Slack频道，用于分享他们的OKR文档和规划文档。人们会上传文档，并在Slack上发布视频回顾主要内容。我们还设定了时长限制。团队会说：“这是我们的OKR，这些是需要关注的重点。”然后，Cal和我会开个马拉松式会议，一起把所有OKR过一遍。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Perfect.
turns.zh: 完美。

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: We used OKRs to drive our processes and we would have the teams present OKRs to us. When the team got too large, it got to be too much time to go through every team's OKR review so we had a Slack channel for each team, their OKRs, a planning channel for each one. And people would post a doc and then a Slack video of going through the major points. And we had a time limit of how long they were allowed to be. And they would say, "Here's our OKRs, here's the things that you would pay attention to." And then Cal and I would do a marathon and we would watch them all together. And-
turns.zh: 我们用OKR来推动流程，团队会向我们汇报OKR。当团队规模过大时，逐一审查每个团队的OKR太耗时了，所以我们为每个团队开设了Slack频道，用于分享他们的OKR文档和规划文档。人们会上传文档，并在Slack上发布视频回顾主要内容。我们还设定了时长限制。团队会说：“这是我们的OKR，这些是需要关注的重点。”然后，Cal和我会开个马拉松式会议，一起把所有OKR过一遍。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: In a room sitting there watching them together?
turns.zh: 在一个房间里一起看吗？

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: Correct. And then we would say, "Do we have any follow-up questions?" And we put in channel our follow-up questions to the team. And sometimes there'd be five to 10 teams that we would then have a follow-up meeting with. We would say that this is a really high priority project or there are a lot of questions that we have, and then we would do a meeting but we were always doing those meetings together. So that was the OKR reviews of getting the alignment. And by asking the questions, we could then ... By it just being us, we could dig into the team. And we each had a chief of staff, so it was the two of us plus our two chiefs of staff, and which they also did a divide and conquer and they worked really well together. They were both long time Slack employees. So for years they had ... One had been an engineering director and one had been a TPM. And then every Monday we had a Monday meeting where we reviewed the progress on the top OKRs and red, yellow, green and don't talk through the green ones, only talk through the red ones and what are the issues. And again, both there. And then we had a weekly meeting with the four of us where we would just go through any issues in the organization, what's going on, what's not.
turns.zh: 对。然后我们会说：“你们还有什么后续问题吗？”我们会在Slack频道向团队提出后续问题。有时会有5到10个团队参加后续会议。我们会说这个项目是高优先级的，或者我们有很多问题，接着就开会讨论。但我们总是一起开会。OKR评审就是要达成共识。通过提问，我们能深入了解团队情况。我们各自都有参谋长，所以是我们两人加上各自的参谋长。他们也分工合作，配合得很好。他们都是Slack的老员工了。多年来，他们一直……一个曾是工程总监，另一个曾是技术项目经理。每周一我们都会开周会，总结主要OKR的进展，标红、黄、绿，不讨论绿色的，只讨论红色的，还有遇到的问题。再然后，我们四人每周开一次会议，讨论组织内的问题，了解动态，解决难题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And the four of us is you, the CTO, the chiefs of staff.
turns.zh: 四人指的是你、CTO和两位参谋长。

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: Yep. And sometimes we would invite people. Like there's an issue with QA, so we'd have the QA leader come in and present to us. But we tried to limit the number of meetings with teams. So it'd be like the Monday meeting was the big meeting that you had to be there and you had to be able to talk to your project and that was it.
turns.zh: 是的。有时我们会邀请其他人。比如QA部门有问题，我们就让QA负责人来汇报。但我们尽量减少与团队的会议次数。所以周一的会议是必须参加的，你得能与自己的项目沟通，仅此而已。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's so much awesomeness here. I love the idea of this Async share your plan in a video instead of meetings with everyone in real time. And you could just do a lot of the stuff Async.
turns.zh: 这里真是太棒了。我喜欢这种异步分享计划的视频，而不是实时开会的做法。很多事情都可以异步处理。

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: We iterated every quarter, just like you iterate on a product. So every quarter we would say did the OKR planning work or not, and then we would adjust. So we got to the point where at one point we added up all the hours of OKR reviews and all the people in them and it was some insane number, like 300 and something and we're like, "This has gotten out of hand." So then we're like, "We have to do something drastic." And that's when we moved them to Async. It was also right after Slack Clips launched.
turns.zh: 我们每个季度都会迭代，就像你迭代产品一样。所以每个季度我们都会评估OKR规划是否有效，如果不达标就会调整策略。曾经有一段时间，我们把所有OKR评审会议的时长和参与人数加起来，数字高得惊人，超过300个小时。我们当时就意识到，情况已经失控了。于是我们决定采取果断措施，将这些会议转移到Async平台上。而这恰好是在Slack Clips功能上线后不久发生的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. That's the video feature. Very cool. Then I know you launched huddles, right? Slack Huddles? Did you use that as a part of this or eventually you just get people into a little huddle asynchronously and talk-
turns.zh: 明白了。这就是视频功能。太棒了。那我知道你们还推出了Huddles功能，对吧？Slack Huddles？你们是把它作为这项改革的一部分，还是最终只是让大家异步开个小会议聊聊？

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: Sometimes. Absolutely. We would be in the reviews and we would huddle with somebody to ask a quick question. We use Huddled all the time. I still do. I love Huddles.
turns.zh: 有时候会。当然会。我们在评审会议中会和某人快速沟通一个问题。我们一直都在用Huddles功能，我现在也还在用。真的很喜欢Huddles。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love it. One crazy thing about Slack is people in Slack don't actually use email internally. It's like all in Slack. It's like the actual vision of Slack working within Slack.
turns.zh: 我也超爱。Slack的一个疯狂之处在于，内部员工基本不发邮件了。所有沟通都在Slack里进行。这正是Slack所倡导的"在Slack内高效协作"的愿景。

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: No email unless you're dealing with somebody external. And no, it's mostly Slack Connect anyway.
turns.zh: 除非是和外部人士沟通，否则基本不发邮件。反正大部分交流都是通过Slack Connect完成的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Anyway. Wow, that's amazing. Okay. I have one more question around product stuff and then I want to talk about AI. So I was reading your newsletter on Substack, which we'll link to and you share this really interesting insight that I've experienced myself that I'll quote you here. One of the mistakes that I see a lot of product managers make is they over index on people who are going to be unhappy with the products they're launching. And basically your advice is not to worry so much about making users unhappy, which I think is counterintuitive to some people. Can you just talk about this lesson and I'd love to hear what product you launched that made people unhappy that you realized, oh, maybe we don't need to worry about this as much.
turns.zh: 好的。哇，太神奇了。好的，我还有一个关于产品方面的提问，然后再聊聊AI。我在Substack上读了你的新闻通讯（我们会附上链接），里面有一个很有趣的见解，我自己也有同感，我这就引用一下。你提到很多产品经理都会过度关注那些可能对新产品不满的用户。你的建议是别太在意让用户不满，这对有些人来说可能有点反直觉。你能详细讲讲这个经验吗？我很想听听你推出的哪个产品让用户不满后，你意识到，哦，或许我们不必太在意这些。

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: I saw it more when you unlaunch things, you take things away there's always some set of users that are using a feature that nobody else does, and then you take it away and they're super unhappy, but there are more people you're going to make happy. So a product manager gets caught in this trap of the vocal minority and the number of people using your product ... Depends on what phase. Are you a Google? Are you Slack? Are you a Glean? But the number of people using your product today is usually unless you're a Google far smaller than the number of people who are going to be using your product tomorrow. So design it for the bigger number of people who are going to be using it tomorrow. If you have to redo the UI and the Who Moved My Cheese, people will be unhappy, but all the new people are going to be like, "This is so much easier." Then do it and deal with the people who are unhappy. (00:47:02): But the trick is you have to be respectful and you have to be transparent and you have to explain. You have to go to people and say, "This is why we made this change." And you have to be authentic. You can't be dismissive and you can't have marketing speak. You have to really say, "Here's for real why." And you have to listen to your audience. You don't want to alienate your early users because most people ... If you made a good decision on why you moved this or why we stopped using Slack calls and moved to Huddles and you have to do it over time and give people choice and then give them enough time to move. So you have to do it in the right way. But if people feel heard, it makes a difference. (00:47:50): I have an example that's not a product example, but I think is a really good one. It's a leadership example. So when I was at Google, there was always a controversy about something, but there was a controversy about ... It was Blogger or something. I can't even remember what it was. It was like we made a change. We were like 50,000 people at the time. There was an engineer in my team, an IT engineer that was super unhappy about the change. And I knew Rachel Whetstone, she was in charge of all of PR and global policy at Google. So huge job. And I emailed Rachel and I'm like, "Hey, do you have an FAQ or something that can help me? Because I don't know why you made this change and that I can help explain to the engineer in my team." (00:48:33): She did not respond to my email. She picked up the phone and she called him. I had no idea she did this. She just called this IT engineer and she listened to him and she heard why he was upset and she explained her reasoning. He was so blown away that she called him that he completely changed his opinion and then he told everyone else in the org. And so it had this effect. And I learned a lot from watching her do that. She never even told me she did it later. She just did it. You just act. You're authentic. You listen to people and you're transparent.
turns.zh: 这种情况在我做产品经理时经常遇到。比如，当你停用某些功能时，总会有一部分用户在使用某个没人用过的功能。然后你把它停用，他们会非常不满，但同时你会让更多人感到满意。因此，产品经理会陷入这样一个困境：一方面要顾及少数发声用户，另一方面要考虑产品使用者的整体数量……这取决于产品所处的阶段。你是谷歌吗？你是Slack吗？你是Glean吗？但目前使用你产品的用户数量通常远远小于未来会使用的用户数量。所以，要为未来更多用户设计产品。如果你必须重做UI或者像《谁动了我的奶酪》那样调整，人们会不高兴，但新用户会觉得“这太简单了”。那就先做，再处理不满的用户。（00:47:02）但关键是要保持尊重、透明，解释清楚。要去跟用户说：“这就是我们做出改变的原因。” 还要保持真诚，不能用营销术语敷衍。必须实话实说，“这就是真实的原因。” 还要倾听用户意见，别疏远早期用户。毕竟大多数人……如果你决定迁移某个功能，或者从Slack通话转向Huddles，这些决策都需要循序渐进，给用户选择的机会，再留出足够的过渡时间。必须谨慎操作。但如果用户感受到被倾听，就会产生积极影响。（00:47:50）我举个非产品相关的例子，但我认为很能说明问题。那是领导力方面的案例。我在谷歌时，曾因某个政策引发争议，比如Blogger之类的。当时我们有5万名员工。我团队里有个IT工程师对某项变更非常不满。我知道谷歌公关和全球政策主管Rachel Whetstone，但她工作繁忙。我给她发邮件说：“嘿，你有没有FAQ之类的资料能帮我？我不知道为什么要做这个变更，能帮我跟团队解释下。” 她没有回复邮件，而是直接打电话给他。我完全不知道她这么做了。她直接打电话给那个IT工程师，倾听他的不满，解释自己的决策理由。他被她的举动深深打动，彻底改变了态度，还在整个组织里宣传此事。这件事对我启发很大。她后来甚至没告诉我她这么做了。她就是行动派，保持真诚，倾听用户，保持透明。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's so funny. This reminds me of a parenting book I'm reading right now that a former guest recommended called Listen. And the core thesis of the book is when your kids are acting up or they're getting off track, so much of what they need is a sense that you're connected to them, a connection which is rooted in you listening to them. And so all-
turns.zh: 太有意思了。这让我想起最近在读的一本育儿书，之前有嘉宾推荐的，叫《倾听》。书的核心观点是，当孩子行为出格或偏离轨道时，他们最需要的是感受到与父母的连接感，而这种连接感的基础就是倾听。换句话说——

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: My favorite parenting book ... I don't know if this is the same one or a different one, it's How to Talk so Your Kids Will Listen & How to Listen so Your Kids Will Talk. Maybe it's the new name of that book, but it's so good and it's so true in everything and also in products. So whether you're in a forum and explaining to customers, whether you're enterprise customers, you're explaining, you're hearing them out, people want to understand.
turns.zh: 我最喜欢的育儿书籍……我不确定这是同一本书还是另一本，但书名是《如何让孩子听你说话》和《如何让孩子说出心里话》。也许这本书换了新书名，但内容非常实用，适用于育儿，也适用于产品设计和客户沟通。无论是在论坛上向客户解释产品，还是面向企业客户进行演示——倾听客户需求、理解他们的诉求，人们都渴望被理解。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. There's so many applications of just the power of listening. Okay. Well, not quite a segue, but let's talk about AI. You're at the epicenter of AI now with Glean. How do you anticipate AI will change our jobs and product? What do you think people may be aren't recognizing it, realizing it? What have you seen?
turns.zh: 太棒了。倾听的力量在诸多场景中都能发挥作用。我们现在正处于AI技术的风口浪尖，Glean公司处于AI领域的核心位置。您如何预见AI将如何改变我们的工作和产品？您认为人们可能尚未充分认识到AI的变革潜力？您见证了哪些变革？

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: I'm going to give you a little bit of my history with AI to get to that point. When AI was a completely different technology stack ... I have a master's in AI. So I started working in AI when ... It's evolved so much. And then of course at Google using it for auto complete and search. It's transformed so many times. But then with this last transformation of GenAI ... And that's what brought me to Glean of seeing this, meeting lots of AI companies and like, "Wow. This is really going to transform how we work." And it's just fascinating seeing these products. I was one of those people like, "Oh yeah, it's going to be so far away." Until I saw GPT3. And I think AI, we are underestimating how much it's going to change how we work. It's not going to be sudden from today to tomorrow because people haven't figured it out yet. They haven't figured out how exactly to leverage it. But the people who have are going to be so far ahead. They're going to be far ahead of everyone else because they're going to be working faster, they're going to be working better. (00:51:33): And in five to 10 years, I think the lines between product managers and engineers and designers are going to blur because AI will enable product managers to build prototypes, to build designs. Designers to build a pro like Figma already has their Figma AI. You can press a button and you can get your initial prototype working. You've got all the co-pilots. So they're not quite there. You still, like with Copilot or with Cursor, you need to be an experienced engineer to know when it's getting it wrong, but they're going to keep getting better. I think people have to be careful about not getting left behind, but their jobs aren't going to go away. They're just going to change. I'm of the believer that we're just going to have a lot more software. But I talked to engineers and to PMs saying, "Yeah, I tried that. It doesn't really work." And then go back to how I worked before. And that's a dangerous spot to be in I think.
turns.zh:
让我先简要分享一下我与AI的渊源。当AI还是一项完全不同的技术栈时……我拥有AI硕士学位，正是在那时开始接触AI领域。AI技术发展迅速，谷歌将其应用于自动补全和搜索功能，历经多次变革。最近，GenAI技术的突破让我深受触动，促使我加入Glean团队。通过接触众多AI公司，我意识到AI将彻底改变我们的工作方式。变革不会一蹴而就，因为人们尚未完全掌握其应用之道。不过先行者必将遥遥领先，他们将以更高效、更优质的方式开展工作。

（00:51:33）未来5到10年，产品经理、工程师和设计师的界限将逐渐模糊。AI将赋予产品经理原型设计和方案构思的能力，如Figma已推出AI功能，点击按钮即可生成初步原型。但目前仍存在局限，比如Copilot或Cursor等工具需要经验丰富的工程师来纠正错误，但这些工具将持续优化。我认为人们必须警惕被时代淘汰，但工作岗位不会消失，只是形式会发生变化。我坚信未来将涌现更多软件应用。但与工程师和产品经理交流时，他们会说：“嗯，我试过了，效果不佳。”然后又回归旧有工作方式。我认为这种停滞心态很危险。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: For people that get anxiety hearing this where they're feeling they're going to be left behind and like, "Oh my God, I don't know enough time to do this or I don't know what I'm doing here." Do you have any advice for what's something someone can do to not fall behind?
turns.zh: 对于那些听完后感到焦虑、担心被淘汰的人，比如“天哪，我没时间学习这些技术，不知道该怎么做”的人，您有什么建议帮助他们不落后？

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: Use the products. This is what good PMs should do period. Always be using new products. It's not a unique thing for AI. When mobile came out, PMs needed to be using mobile apps all the time to try them out, see what the UIs are, see what's working and what isn't. And the same goes even more for AI. Use ChatGPT. If your organization has Glean, use Glean. Use Claude. Try them all. Try them and see what they do. I was talking to a product manager I know who is more forward-thinking and loves playing with new products and he had this use case that blew me away. So he said ... And this was a couple of months ago, so before ... It was right when Gemini had expanded the context window. So his product had a Discord channel and he took the transcript from the Discord channel, which was huge. And he fed it into Gemini the entire channel and then used it to ask questions. Like what is the sentiment of my product? What is the most requested feature? What are the things people are unhappy with? This never would've occurred to me. It's like, that is so smart. And he's like, "It was like a goldmine." Do you know how long it would've taken him to read? And he just wouldn't have done it. (00:54:06): So think about for the argument, oh, I'm too busy. Well, if you use these products it's going to be a leverage on your time. So you get a lot of articles sent to you, summarize them, use AI to summarize the articles. We use Gong at Glean to record all our sales calls. We have a Glean app that will read all the Gong transcripts, put them in a spreadsheet in a certain format of who the AE is, etc. And then summarize all the top requested features from all the Gong calls. And it took a while to get it right. At first the summarization, the prompt wasn't good enough and would give us features that our salespeople would recommend and didn't distinguish that this was actually the customer. So you have to tweak it. It's not going to work out of the box. But then we got it to the point where it worked and these things really save time and you have to use your creative juices as a PM to figure out how it can help you and have patience to iterate and keep trying because the models that we have today can do a lot already.
turns.zh:
使用这些产品。这才是优秀的产品经理应该做的，无需多言。始终要不断尝试新产品。这对AI领域来说并非独有。移动端兴起时，产品经理需要不断使用移动应用来测试UI，观察哪些功能有效，哪些有待改进。对于AI领域更是如此。使用ChatGPT。如果你的公司有Glean，就用Glean。试用Claude。多多尝试，观察其效果。  

我曾与一位思维前瞻、热爱探索新产品的PM交流。他提到的用例让我惊叹不已。几个月前（在Gemini扩展上下文窗口之前），他的团队在Discord频道收集了大量对话记录，并将其导入Gemini进行提问，比如“用户对我的产品反馈如何？”“最受期待的功能是什么？用户不满的点在哪里？”这些思路我从未想过。简直太聪明了！他说：“这简直是金矿。”要知道，手动阅读这些内容得花多长时间？而用AI就能轻松实现。  

对于那些以“太忙”为借口的PM们，我想说——使用这些工具反而能节省时间。比如Gong在Glean中的应用：我们用它录制销售通话，并通过Glean将转录内容整理成表格，标注AE姓名等信息，同时汇总所有通话中提及的高频需求。最初模型生成的需求与销售建议混淆，需要反复调整优化。但现在效果显著，节省了大量时间。作为PM，要发挥创造力挖掘工具价值，并耐心迭代，因为现有模型已能处理诸多场景。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I love your example of the PM and what they did with the Discord channel. Is there anything else along those lines that either you've done to leverage some AI tool to be more productive or folks in your team have done to be more productive youth, either your product leaders or other folks?
turns.zh: 是啊。你举的Discord频道案例太棒了。还有其他类似的案例吗？比如你或团队成员如何利用AI工具提高效率？无论是产品负责人，还是其他成员。

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: So many examples. So one that I did really recently is I wrote a prompt in Glean to help me get the status of features. And we have a Launch Cal, and you can look at Launch Cal it'll say a date. But then is it really the date? What are the outstanding issues? So it will look at our Launch Cal and it will see if there are any open year tickets, what the Slack conversations are and the customers who are beta testing it, bring all these together to tell me, okay, launch date is this according to Launch Cal, but here are all the open issues and here are the open conversations that people are talking about. So then it can give me the confidence level of the future looking. So I can run the prompt, just put in the name of the feature. So I don't have to read all of these channels. (00:56:28): So this is a prompt that I built two weeks ago because we're advancing our prompting capabilities. And so I was testing it out and I was like, "Ooh, I could do this." So that's another example and engineers are using it for automating part of the incident management of I got an incident, how do I see were their previous incidents that were similar to it, where they're not. And so these are the type of things you can look at to help you. But the simplest, simplest is there's so much news. Let me just paste in all of these things and summarize them. As a product manager at Gleam, here are all the latest news. What do I have to care about? What's impacting me and potentially competitive to any of the products that I have?
turns.zh: 例子太多了。最近我做的一个例子是，在Glean中写了一个提示，帮助我了解功能的状态。我们有Launch Cal，你可以查看Launch Cal，它会显示一个日期。但这真的是日期吗？还有哪些未解决的问题？于是它会查看我们的Launch Cal，查看是否有未关闭的年票，Slack对话记录，以及正在进行测试的客户，把这些信息整合起来，告诉我，根据Launch Cal，发布日期应该是这个时间，但这里还有所有未解决的问题，以及人们正在讨论的相关对话。这样就能让我对未来的情况更有信心了。我只需要运行这个提示，输入功能名称，就不用去浏览所有这些频道了。（00:56:28）：这是我两周前开发的一个提示，因为我们正在提升我们的提示功能。当时我在测试它，我想，"哦，我可以用这个。"这就是另一个例子，工程师们用它来自动化部分事件管理流程。比如我接到一个事件，该怎么看之前类似的事件呢？哪些是相似的，哪些不是？这些都是可以帮助你的事情。但最简单的，最简单的是，有太多新闻了。让我把所有这些内容都粘贴进来，然后总结一下。作为Glean的产品经理，以下是所有最新消息。我需要关注什么？哪些会影响我？对我现有产品的竞争力又如何？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And putting that into say Claude or ChatGPT you're saying.
turns.zh: 然后把它输入到Claude或者ChatGPT里，你就会得到结果。

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I think that beginning of the prompt is something a lot of people don't know is the power of just giving it a role like you are a product manager at Gleam. From that perspective, give me this summary versus just summarize this and that ends up being really powerful right.
turns.zh: 是的。我觉得这个提示的开头是很多人不知道的，就是给它一个角色，比如你是在Glean担任产品经理。从这个角度出发，给我这个总结，而不是简单地总结，这真的很有效。

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: A hundred percent. And you can compare what is Claude's PR saying that ... They just launched Claude Enterprise. How is Claude Enterprise different from OpenAI Enterprise? Again, you can do it yourself, but these micro improvements in your productivity help. For my newsletter, I interviewed Claire Vo who came out with ChatPRD. And so product managers are using is. We're just starting to evaluate it internally, so I haven't personally used it yet, but it's super cool and you can use ChatGPT to do a PRD. And ChatPRD, it's more templatized and more frameworks of how to do that. And again, these things are going to keep getting better.
turns.zh: 百分之百同意。你可以比较Claude的PR说了什么……他们刚刚推出了Claude Enterprise。Claude Enterprise和OpenAI Enterprise有什么不同？再说一次，你可以自己做，但这些微小的生产力提升确实有帮助。就我的新闻通讯而言，我采访了Claire Vo，她推出了ChatPRD。产品经理们正在使用它。我们刚刚开始内部评估，所以我个人还没用过，但它真的很酷，你可以用ChatGPT来做PRD。而ChatPRD，更模板化，更有框架指导如何做这些事情。再说一次，这些东西会不断改进。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Claire's been on the podcast, she's going to be speaking at the Lenny and Friends Summit coming up October 24th.
turns.zh: Claire上过播客了，她即将在10月24日参加Lenny and Friends峰会。

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: Oh, cool.
turns.zh: 哦，太酷了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. A crazy stat she shared. She's making six figures off this product that she builds on the weekends ChatPRD.
turns.zh: 是的。她分享了一个疯狂的数据。她在周末开发的ChatPRD这个产品，每个月就能赚六位数。

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: So cool.
turns.zh: 太酷了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Incredible.
turns.zh: 难以置信。

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: But it also shows what you can build with AI.
turns.zh: 但这也展示了你用AI能做什么。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Right. It's just her. I think she just recently hired some engineers to help because she has three kids CTO at LaunchDarkly and just is building this on the side making a hundred thousand plus dollars. Incredible. I want to add a couple of things here. So one is for folks looking for ideas for how to use AI tooling for their PM job. There's a couple of posts I've written that I'll link to in the show notes just to put that out there of just a bunch of PM sharing, here's what I've done with these various tools. Another thought I'd love to get your take on. There's a lot of fear that the PM job be replaced by AI. And I've recently realized that it's the opposite. I think the PM role is the best positioned to thrive in the world of AI because if you just think about you have a tool that can just build a thing for you, just like you're staring at this blank thing that can build anything for you, which function would you think would have the best chance of asking it of what to build and how to articulate what to build best? (00:59:47): To me, it's clearly Product People. They're best at figuring out what to build, what matters most, where the impact's going to be what customers need. Not to say other functions don't also have the skills, but I feel like of all functions, PMs have the most of that specific skill. I'd love to get your take on that.
turns.zh: 好的。就是她了。我觉得她最近雇了些工程师帮忙，因为她有三个孩子。她是LaunchDarkly的CTO，目前只是在业余时间开发这个项目，每年能赚十多万美元。太不可思议了。我还想补充几点。这里有几位朋友可能想了解如何将AI工具应用于产品经理工作中。我写过几篇相关文章，会在节目笔记里附上链接，里面都是产品经理们分享如何利用这些工具的经验。另外，我很想听听大家对AI取代产品经理工作的担忧。我最近意识到情况恰恰相反。我认为产品经理角色在AI时代最有可能蓬勃发展，因为如果你想象一个工具能为你自动搭建东西，就像你面对一个能为你构建任何东西的空白界面一样，你觉得哪个功能最有可能指导它该建什么，以及如何最有效地表达需求？（00:59:47）对我来说，显然是产品团队。他们最擅长确定要构建什么、什么最重要、影响力在哪里，以及客户的需求是什么。不是说其他职能没有这些能力，但我觉得在所有职能中，产品经理最擅长这些技能。我很想听听大家对此的看法。

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: That. I think that AI, the one thing it's not good at is being creative. So if you're a PM who's doing the grout work, it's going to take your job away. But if you're a PM who actually is strategic and can pull the pieces together and be creative and think how you do something that it's going to differentiate. Because it's not going to give you that leak. It'll say, here's what customers are asking for, here are the problems today, but you have to figure out how to solve it. So in some ways it might weed out the good from the bad PMs. Because there are a significant number of PMs who are more just execution. And I think that part of the job hopefully will be lowered because I hope a lot more of the execution will be able to automate updating Jira and all these things that just take time and creating even little Launch Cals, which PMs have to do manually now. So hopefully a lot of that work goes away and then people can be more creative. And I think designers and PMs are going to blend because the best designers I've worked with are product thinkers and a lot of really good PMs can also design. It depends on what kind of product you're PMing for. So I agree with the caveat that it will become harder to be a great PM.
turns.zh: 是的。我认为AI不擅长创造性思维。所以如果你是做琐碎工作的产品经理，AI会取代你的工作。但如果你是一个具有战略眼光、能整合资源、善于创新、善于思考如何创造差异的产品经理，AI就无法替代你。因为它不会给你提供灵感，它只会告诉你客户的需求是什么，当前存在哪些问题，但你得自己想办法解决。所以在某种程度上，AI可能会淘汰不合格的产品经理，因为确实有很多产品经理只是在做执行工作。希望这部分工作能自动化，比如更新Jira之类的，还有现在产品经理手动做的很多小任务，比如创建Launch Calls。这样一来，产品经理就能腾出更多时间去创新了。我觉得设计师和产品经理会融合起来，因为我合作过的最优秀的设计师都是产品思考者，而很多优秀的产品经理也能胜任设计工作。当然，这取决于你负责的产品类型。所以我同意你的观点，成为优秀的产品经理会变得更难。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wait, say more about that. It'll be harder to be a great PM because many PMs are doing things that are mostly project management and that's the stuff that-
turns.zh: 等等，请详细说说。为什么成为优秀的产品经理会更难？因为很多产品经理做的工作大多是项目管理，而这些工作——

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: Yeah. Let me rephrase. It's not going to be harder to be a great PM, but to be a PM, the not so good PMs jobs will go away. The great PMs will still have great jobs.
turns.zh: 是的。让我重新表述一下。成为优秀的产品经理不会更难，但对于不那么优秀的产品经理来说，他们的工作岗位会消失。优秀的产品经理仍然会有很好的工作机会。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I totally hear you. So in a sense there might be fewer. You might need fewer PMs, but I think that applies in theory to every function. Fewer engineers. Fewer designers.
turns.zh: 是的。我完全理解你的意思。所以从某种意义上说，可能职位会减少。你可能需要更少的产品经理，但我认为这在理论上适用于每个职能。工程师会减少，设计师也会减少。

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: I don't think you'll need fewer. I think you'll be able to do more things. Think about every company. Our head of sales came to me the other day, "You need to hire more engineers because we just have so many things we need to build." I'm like, "When have you ever worked in a company where you thought that you didn't need more engineers?" You always want people to build more stuff. So I don't think you're going to need fewer. I think you're just going to get so much more done.
turns.zh: 我觉得你们不需要减少人员。我认为你们能做更多事情。想想每家公司吧。前几天我们的销售主管来找我：“你得多招些工程师，因为我们有太多需要开发的东西了。” 我反问：“你什么时候在公司里觉得不需要更多工程师了？” 你总是希望团队能开发出更多产品。所以我觉得你们不需要减少人员。相反，你们能完成更多工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A lot of people are building AI into their product. Glean is obviously an example which integrates LLMs, which innately are non-deterministic and hard to know if they're going to provide anything good. Sometimes something really dumb comes out. Do you have any advice on working with these very complicated systems that don't necessarily ... You can't control and building them into your products? Anything you've learned that might be helpful?
turns.zh: 现在很多人都在把人工智能融入自己的产品。Glean显然就是一个例子，它集成了大语言模型（LLM），而LLM本质上是不确定性很强的，很难预测它们能否提供有用的输出。有时候甚至会得到一些很离谱的结果。对于这些复杂得难以控制、又要集成到产品中的系统，你有什么建议吗？有没有什么经验可以分享？

turns.speaker: Tamar Yehoshua
turns.en: My first week at Glean was eye-opening in learning some of these things. But let me first just explain what Glean does for people who may not know. So Glean was started as enterprise search. Glean reads content of all your SaaS apps. So it reads the content from Microsoft, Google, Slack, Salesforce, Jira, like any SaaS tool that you use, it indexes it and enables you to search. So it started as just enterprise search and using AI. So it was an AI search using BERT models and using vector embeddings in 2019. Because the early engineers at Glean came from Google and Google created BERT to enhance search. And so it was obvious that they would be using ML techniques for search. Then GPT3 came along and added a natural language interface, a chat interface.
